questions.stem: Which pair of set phrases opens and closes a formal Japanese letter?
options: 「はいけい」 … 「さようなら」
「こんにちは」 … 「けいぐ」
「はいけい」 … 「けいぐ」
「けいぐ」 … 「はいけい」
questions.explanation: 「はいけい」 ('respectfully') opens a formal letter and 「けいぐ」 ('yours sincerely') closes it; the two are a fixed pair. 「さようなら」 is a spoken farewell and never ends a formal letter.

questions.stem: In a formal letter, what usually comes straight after 「はいけい」?
options: The writer's full name and home address
The date and the reader's postal address
A summary of the request being made
A remark about the season or the weather
questions.explanation: Japanese letters open with a seasonal greeting, then ask after the reader's health before reaching the main business. The writer's name and the date come at the end, not the start.

questions.stem: You are writing a letter from Melbourne in July. Which seasonal opening suits it?
options: 「すずしくなって、秋らしくなりました。」
「さむい日がつづいていますが、お元気ですか。」
「あつい日がつづいていますが、お元気ですか。」
「さくらの花がきれいなきせつになりました。」
questions.explanation: July is winter in Australia, so a greeting about cold days fits. The seasonal greeting describes the writer's own season, even though July is summer for a reader in Japan.

questions.stem: Which sentence usually closes a personal letter or email?
options: 「おひさしぶりです。お元気ですか。」
「お手紙ありがとう。うれしかったです。」
「では、お体に気をつけてください。」
「はじめまして。どうぞよろしく。」
questions.explanation: Wishing the reader good health, 「お体に気をつけてください」, is a standard way to end a letter. Introducing yourself, asking after the reader and thanking them for their letter all belong at the start.

questions.stem: Emi is writing a personal letter to her friend Ken. How does she sign off at the end?
options: 「ケンより」
「ケンさまへ」
「エミより」
「エミへ」
questions.explanation: 「より」 ('from') follows the writer's name at the end of a personal letter, and 「へ」 ('to') follows the reader's name at the top: 「ケンさんへ」 … 「エミより」. Putting 「へ」 after your own name addresses the letter to yourself.

questions.stem: You are emailing a Japanese host family you have never met. Which opening is appropriate?
options: 「お元気でしたか。エマでした。」
「はじめまして。エマともうします。」
「やあ、エマだよ。元気？」
「ひさしぶり！エマです。」
questions.explanation: 「はじめまして」 is for a first contact, and 「〜ともうします」 is the humble way to give your name to people you have not met. 「ひさしぶり」 means you have met before, and 「やあ」 … 「だよ」 is far too casual.

questions.stem: Which sentence closes a formal email that asks a favour?
options: 「どうもありがとう。じゃあね。」
「では、また来週会おうね。バイバイ。」
「おねがいだから、早くしてね。」
「どうぞよろしくおねがいいたします。」
questions.explanation: 「よろしくおねがいいたします」 is the set phrase that closes a request, and 「いたします」 makes it humble. The others are casual phrases used with friends.

questions.stem: On the envelope of a formal letter, which title follows the reader's name?
options: くん
ちゃん
より
さま
questions.explanation: 「さま」 is the respectful title used on envelopes and in formal letters, for customers and people you do not know well. 「くん」 and 「ちゃん」 are for friends and children, and 「より」 means 'from'.

questions.stem: Which style is normally used for a formal essay or report?
options: The polite 「です」/「ます」 style
Casual speech with 「よ」 and 「ね」
Humble 「けいご」 throughout
The plain 「だ」/「である」 style
questions.explanation: Essays, reports and articles for a general readership are usually written in the plain 「だ」/「である」 style. 「です」/「ます」 suits letters, speeches and writing addressed directly to a reader.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written in the 「である」 style?
options: 「かんきょうをまもることはたいせつだよね。」
「かんきょうをまもることはたいせつでしょうね。」
「かんきょうをまもることはたいせつである。」
「かんきょうをまもることはたいせつです。」
questions.explanation: 「である」 replaces 「だ」 or 「です」 at the end of a noun or な-adjective sentence in formal writing. 「です」 is the polite style, and 「よね」 and 「ね」 are spoken particles that do not belong in an essay.

questions.stem: How is 「このもんだいはむずかしいです。」 written in the plain 「だ」/「である」 style?
options: 「このもんだいはむずかしいである。」
「このもんだいはむずかしいだ。」
「このもんだいはむずかしいでした。」
「このもんだいはむずかしい。」
questions.explanation: An い-adjective needs nothing after it in plain style, so 「です」 is simply dropped. 「だ」 and 「である」 follow nouns and な-adjectives, not い-adjectives, and 「むずかしいでした」 is a common error for 「むずかしかったです」.

questions.stem: Which text would normally use plain forms with spoken particles such as 「よ」 and 「ね」?
options: An application for a part-time job
An email to a close friend
A formal letter to a school principal
A report for the school newsletter
questions.explanation: Writing to a close friend imitates casual speech, so plain forms with 「よ」 and 「ね」 are natural. A formal letter and a job application need 「です」/「ます」 and polite set phrases, and a report uses the plain 「である」 style without spoken particles.

questions.stem: Which opening suits a speech to a school assembly?
options: 「本レポートでは、かんきょうもんだいについて次のようにまとめる。」
「はいけい。さむい日がつづいていますが、お元気ですか。」
「みなさん、こんにちは。今日はかんきょうについてお話しします。」
「やあ、みんな！今日はかんきょうの話だよ。よろしく！」
questions.explanation: A speech greets the audience directly with 「みなさん」 and uses 「です」/「ます」, often with the humble 「お話しします」 to introduce the topic. 「次のようにまとめる」 is report language, and 「やあ…だよ」 is too casual for an assembly.

questions.stem: Which sentence would end a speech?
options: 「ごせいちょう、ありがとうございました。」
「では、これからはじめます。」
「今日は、このテーマについてお話しします。」
「はいけい、春らしくなりました。」
questions.explanation: 「ごせいちょう、ありがとうございました」 thanks the audience for listening and is the standard close of a speech. The others open a speech or a letter.

questions.stem: Which features mark a journal entry (「にっき」)?
options: First person, past tense, personal feelings and a date
A headline, third person and facts for a wide readership
Headings, a neutral tone and findings with a recommendation
Questions and answers between two named speakers
questions.explanation: A journal entry records the writer's own day and feelings, usually in the plain style because it is written for oneself, under a date. Headlines belong to articles, and headings with findings to reports.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a review?
options: To set out the results of a survey without any opinion
To describe something and give a judgement or recommendation
To record the writer's feelings about their day for themselves
To tell an invented story with characters and a plot
questions.explanation: A review of a film, book, restaurant or product describes it and evaluates it, often ending with a recommendation such as 「ぜひ見てください」. A survey report presents findings, not the writer's verdict.

questions.stem: Which sentence would most likely appear in a report?
options: 「みなさん、スマホを使いすぎないでください！おねがいします！」
「アンケートによると、高校生の六十パーセントが毎日スマホを三時間いじょう使っている。」
「スマホって、ほんとうにべんりだよね！みんなもそう思うでしょう？」
「今日はスマホをなくして、一日中とてもかなしい気持ちだった。」
questions.explanation: A report presents findings objectively, often citing a survey with 「〜によると」, in the plain 「である」 style. The others are casual speech, a journal entry and a direct appeal to an audience.

questions.stem: Which feature is typical of an article for a magazine or newspaper?
options: A title and an opening that draws in a wide readership
A greeting to one reader and a closing set phrase
A date at the top and the writer's private feelings
Lines of dialogue showing who speaks in each turn
questions.explanation: An article has a title, often subheadings, and an engaging opening for readers the writer does not know. Greetings and closing phrases mark a letter, and a date with private feelings marks a journal.

questions.stem: You are writing up an interview with a Japanese athlete. Which question suits the interviewer?
options: 「どうしてこのスポーツを始めたのだろうか。」
「どうしてこのスポーツを始めたんですか。」
「どうしてこのスポーツを始めたの？」
「どうしてこのスポーツを始めた。」
questions.explanation: An interviewer speaks politely to the person being interviewed, and 「んですか」 asks for an explanation naturally. Plain 「の？」 is for friends, and 「〜のだろうか」 is essay language, where a writer poses a question to the reader.

questions.stem: Which features mark a story?
options: Arguments for one side and a call to action
Past-tense narration, characters and direct speech in 「」
Headings, statistics and a neutral recommendation
A greeting, a request and a closing set phrase
questions.explanation: A story narrates events, usually in the past, with characters whose words appear as direct speech in 「」. It belongs to the imaginative style, unlike a report (informative) or a persuasive piece.

questions.stem: In a role-play about weekend plans, which reply acknowledges the other speaker's view before disagreeing?
options: 「そうですね。じゃ、またあとで話しましょう。」
「たしかにそうですね。でも、雨がふったらどうしますか。」
「いいえ、ちがいます。それはぜったいにだめです。」
「だから、私の考えのほうが正しいと言いましたよ。」
questions.explanation: 「たしかにそうですね」 accepts the other person's point before 「でも」 raises a concern, a polite way to disagree in Japanese. A flat 「いいえ、ちがいます」 sounds confrontational, and 「またあとで話しましょう」 puts the issue off without engaging with it.

questions.stem: Which sentence offers a compromise?
options: 「土曜日は出かけるつもりだと、前にも言いましたよ。」
「じゃ、土曜日は勉強して、日曜日に出かけるのはどうですか。」
「土曜日も日曜日も、ぜったいに出かけたくありません。」
「どうして日曜日にどうしても出かけたいんですか。」
questions.explanation: 「〜のはどうですか」 proposes an option, and splitting the weekend meets both people halfway. Asking why seeks information, and 「ぜったいに」 refuses any compromise.

questions.stem: At the end of a role-play, which sentence confirms the agreed outcome?
options: 「日曜日の天気よほうは、たしか雨だそうですよ。」
「じゃ、日曜日に出かけるということにしましょう。」
「日曜日に出かけるかどうか、まだわかりません。」
「日曜日に出かけるのは、ちょっと…。」
questions.explanation: 「〜ということにしましょう」 settles on a decision and confirms it for both speakers. 「ちょっと…」 is a soft refusal left unfinished, which reopens the issue rather than closing it.

questions.stem: What is the main aim of persuasive writing?
options: To convince the reader to accept a view or take action
To weigh up several views fairly and reach a judgement
To entertain the reader with an imagined world
To give the reader facts without the writer's opinion
questions.explanation: Persuasive writing argues for one position and tries to move the reader, using techniques such as rhetorical questions and 「〜べきだ」. Weighing several views fairly is evaluative writing.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a rhetorical question typical of persuasive Japanese?
options: 「この本はいくらでしたか。」
「このままでいいのだろうか。」
「今、何時ですか。」
「明日はどこに行くの？」
questions.explanation: 「〜のだろうか」 poses a question the writer does not expect the reader to answer, inviting them to agree that something must change. The others are ordinary questions asking for information.

questions.stem: Which feature marks evaluative writing rather than persuasive writing?
options: It argues for one side only and urges the reader to act
It tells an invented story with characters and a plot
It records the writer's personal feelings about a day
It presents both sides fairly before reaching a conclusion
questions.explanation: Evaluative writing compares positions, aligns like points and justifies a conclusion, often with 「一方」 and 「〜といういけんもある」. Persuasive writing argues for one side only.

questions.stem: Which writing style describes an imagined situation with characters and a plot?
options: Imaginative
Informative
Evaluative
Persuasive
questions.explanation: Imaginative writing creates a story or situation, often with direct speech, description and the past tense. Informative writing presents facts, and evaluative writing weighs up ideas.

questions.stem: A student writes about how a stay with a host family in Osaka changed the way she thinks. Which writing style is this?
options: Evaluative
Persuasive
Personal
Informative
questions.explanation: Personal writing reflects on the writer's own experiences and feelings, usually in the first person. It is not informative, because the focus is the writer's response rather than facts for the reader.

questions.stem: Which connective introduces the second point after 「まず」?
options: 「つまり」
「しかし」
「このように」
「次に」
questions.explanation: 「まず」 ('first'), 「次に」 ('next') and 「さらに」 ('furthermore') set points out in order. 「つまり」 rephrases, 「しかし」 contrasts and 「このように」 sums up at the end.

questions.stem: What does 「一方」 do in an essay?
options: Rephrases the same point: 'in other words'
Adds a further point: 'furthermore, moreover'
Introduces the other side: 'on the other hand'
Gives an example of the point: 'for instance'
questions.explanation: 「一方」 ('on the other hand') sets a second view or fact against the first, which makes it central to evaluative writing. 'In other words' is 「つまり」, and 'furthermore' is 「さらに」.

questions.stem: Which connective completes 「スマホはとてもべんりだ。___、使いすぎるとけんこうにわるい。」?
options: 「まず」
「しかし」
「さらに」
「つまり」
questions.explanation: The second sentence contrasts with the first (useful, but harmful if overused), so the connective is 「しかし」, 'however'. 「さらに」 would add a further point in the same direction.

questions.stem: Which connective completes 「ねる前にスマホを使うと、よくねむれない。___、ねる前のスマホはけんこうによくないのだ。」?
options: 「まず」
「つまり」
「一方」
「しかし」
questions.explanation: The second sentence restates the first as a general conclusion, so 「つまり」 ('in other words, in short') fits, and 「のだ」 marks it as the explanation. 「一方」 and 「しかし」 would introduce a contrast that is not there.

questions.stem: Where in an essay does 「このように」 usually appear?
options: In the conclusion, summing up the points made
In the first line, introducing the topic
Before a quotation, introducing what someone said
Before an example, introducing a specific case
questions.explanation: 「このように」 ('in this way, as shown above') gathers up the preceding points to lead into the conclusion. An example is introduced by 「たとえば」.

questions.stem: What does 「さらに」 signal?
options: A conclusion drawn from all the points
The first point in a sequence
A further point in the same direction
A contrast with the previous point
questions.explanation: 「さらに」 means 'furthermore' or 'moreover' and strengthens an argument by adding a point. A contrast is 「しかし」 or 「一方」, and a first point is 「まず」.

questions.stem: Which particle completes 「先生は『明日テストがあります』___ 言いました。」?
options: と
を
が
に
questions.explanation: The quotation particle 「と」 marks the words that were said, in direct speech inside 『』 or 「」 and in reported speech alike. 「を」 cannot mark a quotation before 「言う」.

questions.stem: How is 「先生は『明日テストがあります』と言いました。」 written as reported speech?
options: 「先生は明日テストがあったと言いました。」
「先生は明日テストがあるを言いました。」
「先生は明日テストがあるそうと言いました。」
「先生は明日テストがあると言いました。」
questions.explanation: Reported speech drops the quotation marks and puts the quoted words in the plain form, keeping their original tense: 「あります」 becomes 「ある」. Shifting it to the past (「あった」), as English does with 'would be', changes the meaning in Japanese.

questions.stem: On 「げんこうようし」, how do you show the start of a new paragraph?
options: Leave a whole line empty between paragraphs
Write the first character in a larger size
Start the paragraph in the middle of a line
Leave the first square of the line empty
questions.explanation: Each new paragraph begins on a new line with the first square left blank. Blank lines are not used between paragraphs.

questions.stem: How many squares does 「きっぷ」 take on 「げんこうようし」?
options: Two
Four
Five
Three
questions.explanation: Small kana such as 「っ」, 「ゃ」 and 「ゅ」 take a square of their own, so 「き」, 「っ」 and 「ぷ」 fill three squares. The small 「っ」 sits in the corner of its square.

questions.stem: On 「げんこうようし」, where does 「。」 go when a sentence ends in the last square of a line?
options: In the first square of the next line
In the second square of the next line
On a new line, after an empty square
In that same last square, with the final character
questions.explanation: Punctuation never starts a line on 「げんこうようし」, so a 「。」 that would fall there is written in the last square with the final character (or just beneath it). Elsewhere 「。」 and 「、」 each take a square of their own.

questions.stem: You are asking your teacher what she did on Sunday. Which question is appropriate?
options: 「先生は日曜日、何をなさいましたか。」
「あなたは日曜日、何をしましたか。」
「先生は日曜日、何をしたの？」
「先生は日曜日、何をいたしましたか。」
questions.explanation: 「なさる」 is the respectful form of 「する」, used for a superior's actions, and a teacher is addressed as 「先生」, not 「あなた」. 「いたす」 is humble, for your own actions, so using it for the teacher is a classic error.

questions.stem: Which sentence humbly gives your own name?
options: 「エマともうします。」
「エマとおっしゃいます。」
「エマといらっしゃいます。」
「エマとなさいます。」
questions.explanation: 「もうす」 is the humble form of 「言う」 and is used for yourself. 「おっしゃる」 is the respectful form for someone else's words, so using it of yourself would raise your own status.

questions.stem: Which verb shows respect in 「田中先生は来週オーストラリアに ___。」?
options: もうします
いらっしゃいます
まいります
いたします
questions.explanation: 「いらっしゃる」 is the respectful form of 「行く」, 「来る」 and 「いる」, used for a superior. 「まいる」 is the humble form of the same verbs, for the speaker's own movements, so it would lower the teacher.
